 Zoo History 
 
 The mission of the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo is to create compelling experiences that connect people and community with wildlife, and inspire personal responsibility for conservation of the natural world. Education. Conservation. Adventure. Community. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 1989Gulf Shores, Alabama entrepreneur Joey Ward builds a small, community zoo on a family-owned parcel of land in the heart of town, a mile from the beach. Zooland Animal Park becomes home to a collection of tropical birds, snakes, big cats and other exotic wildlife, run by a small staff of zookeepers. While Zooland is extremely popular with locals and vacationers, Gulf Shores isn’t the tourist hot spot it is today, and the zoo is only a seasonal attraction. However, Joey and his parents, Wade and Pat Ward, are devoted custodians of the zoo’s animals. 
 
 
 
 1991The Ward family forms a non-profit charitable organization, The Zoo Foundation, Inc. to operate the park, and the Wards continue their generosity and dedication to the zoo. 
 
 
 
 1995Alabama transplant Patti Hall walks through the gates of the zoo to become a volunteer. Her passion for animals and professional credentials in management, administration, education and public communications puts her on a path that will dramatically change the zoo’s fate forever. 
 
 
 
 1997Joey Ward and the Zoo Board of Directors asks Patti Hall to take over as Zoo Director. The following year, while running a zoo now filled with hundreds of animals, Patti faces her first big challenge living on the Gulf Coast, with the arrival of Hurricane Georges. Realizing that yearly tropical storm season is a new way of life, her dedication to the zoo’s animals means that their safety and security takes precedence over everything else. Little does she know the true test she will face a few years later. 
 
 
 
 1999Patti hires Cyndi Johnson as Head Zookeeper who will later become the zoo’s Curator. Patti’s primary responsibility is to keep the zoo operational and open during tourist seasoning in order to make enough money during the spring and summer months to survive through fall and winter, the off-season. She holds raffles, bake sales, even raids zoo vending machines to pay the bills, feed and care for the animals and stay operational. 
 
 
 
 2000Patti and the Board decide to rename the zoo to bring more credibility and prestige to the organization. The Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo is officially born. Each tourist season, Patti launches various zoo programs, including: educational animal visits to schools and libraries, community events, and promotions aimed at tourists. She turns “Boo in the Zoo” into a monster Halloween hit drawing over 2,500 annual attendees, and makes many improvements to animal exhibits, the gift shop, and the facility grounds. 
 
 
 
 2004By the end of summer, the zoo has its best season ever. Then, an unbelievable twist hits the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo and turns its world upside down and inside out. On Monday, September 13th, CBS news anchor Dan Rather announces that a deadly Category 3 hurricane named Ivan is heading toward the Alabama coast. Gulf Shores will likely be the bullseye, and a mandatory evacuation has been ordered for thousands of residents. But what about hundreds of zoo animals? 
 
 
 
 2004- ContinuedPatti is certain they will not survive the deadly storm if they are left behind. No US zoo has ever been completely evacuated for a natural disaster, until the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo. Over 36 hours, Patti and her staff pack up over 265 animals and transport them 20 miles inland to her home and property where they, her staff’s families, and their pets, all hunker down to wait out Hurricane Ivan. There is one animal they must leave behind - the zoo’s mascot, Chuckie, the 11-ft. 1,000 lb. American alligator who they hope will survive in his swampy exhibit. 
 
 
 
 2004- ContinuedOn September 16th, Hurricane Ivan makes landfall. The Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo is completely destroyed and under 14 feet of water from the Gulf of Mexico. The towns of Gulf Shores and Orange Beach are also demolished. In the aftermath back at Patti’s house, there is no municipal power or running water, cell and telephone service are down, and they have a very limited supply of food and bottled water for the staff and the animals. 
 
 
 
 2004- ContinuedThey are completely dependent on a few small generators and cut off from all emergency services. The temperature and humidity are in the high 90’s to add to the misery. In spite of the direness, they had all survived the worst natural disaster to hit the Gulf Coast in 25 years. Yet, the animals of the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo are now all homeless, and Patti’s staff has no idea if their own homes are still standing. But not one animal life is lost in the transport or during the relocation, and no zookeeper has been injured, except for Patti who received a monkey bite on her finger. The bond between animals and keepers during this extraordinary undertaking is beyond description. 
 
 
 
 2004- ContinuedIn the aftermath of Hurricane Ivan, word spreads about Patti’s historic rescue mission and for the zoo’s desperate search for Chuckie, the alligator who has gone missing. The national media comes calling. NatGeo, People magazine, The Weather Channel, CNN, Good Morning America, local TV and radio stations and countless newspapers report on and interview Patti. Lifting their spirits, Chuckie is found safe and sound, and this little zoo in Alabama becomes a big story. 
 
 
 
 2004- ContinuedIt is one particular appearance that starts Patti and the zoo on another fateful journey no one would ever believe possible. A few days after the evacuation, Peter Jennings of ABC World News features Patti as his Person of the Week, “…And so we hail Patti Hall…shelter from the storm.” As it happens, Los Angeles documentary TV producer Julie Leifermann watches the segment and makes note of this compelling story. 
 
 
 
 2005Six months after the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo has survived Hurricane Ivan, TV Producer Leifermann looks up Patti and the zoo and finds that they are struggling to rebuild the zoo facility, but the animals are all there, happy and healthy. Within weeks, a 13-episode TV series is developed and sold to Animal Planet and Leifermann’s L.A. production company converges on Gulf Shores to bring this heroic and touching tale to a global broadcast audience.At the start of shooting, they all endure two more evacuations for Hurricanes Dennis and Katrina, but Patti and her staff are determined, in spite of setbacks, to complete the rebuild and reopen the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo. 
 
 
 
 2006On February 15th The Little Zoo That Could debuts on primetime TV and America falls in love with Patti Hall, her amazing zookeepers, and about 300 of the most charming zoo animals you could ever meet. Monetary donations pour in as viewers witness the inspiring dedication of Patti and her staff lovingly care for their animals while attempting a comeback of the zoo. Hope turns into triumph and the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo is able to open its doors only 14 months after being completely destroyed. It becomes known as The Little Zoo, a “must-see” place on the map, and tourism comes roaring back to the town of Gulf Shores and its neighboring communities still recovering from the hurricanes. By the end of 2006, the zoo has the most successful season in its history. 
 
 
 
 2007Life is still precarious. June to November is hurricane season. The reconstructed zoo sitting atop swampland covered in sand on a barrier island cannot survive another powerful storm. It is a ticking time bomb. The only long-term solution is to move to safer terrain and build a new zoo. An impossibly expensive, complicated dream. But thanks to another Gulf Shores family, this isn’t going to be a far-fetched dream. Animal-lovers Clyde Weir and his daughter Andrea are deeply touched by The Little Zoo TV series and want to help in a big way.  
 
 
 
 2007-ContinuedThey stun Patti with a gift to the zoo of 25 acres of prime Gulf Shores real estate located four miles off the island. However, designing and building a new multi-million dollar facility is a complicated endeavor, and over the ensuing years, the enormous resources and commitments required by a non-profit zoo, make it very difficult. By 2008, The Great Recession adds to this challenge. 
 
 
 
 2010The worse man-made disaster to hit the Gulf, the Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill puts Patti’s dream zoo into a deep freeze. The beach communities of Alabama take a devastating hit from the spill, as do their tourism business. Fundraising for a new zoo comes to a grinding halt. Coping with yet another disaster, Patti is determined to keep the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo viable. 
 
 
 
 2011In a brilliant attempt to raise awareness about the environmental impact the oil spill had on wildlife, the new zoo team developed a design concept that would place the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo at the forefront of conservation and sustainability as a fully operational green zoo. But again, their efforts to raise enough capital were hampered by slow economic recovery. This ambitious plan was not to be. But as they always did under Patti’s leadership, they re-grouped and continued to build on the current zoo’s success. 
 
 
 
 2014An important alliance is made with renowned animal expert Jim Fowler who assists Patti with a more feasible design path for the new zoo. In another amazing twist of fate, Joey Ward, the same person who built Zooland Animal Park meets Jim Fowler. Twenty-seven years later, Wade and Pat Ward financially jumpstart another new zoo construction project. 
 
 
 
 2016Joey Ward is overseeing construction of the new Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo in its new location and Patti Hall is on the brink of living her dream - The Little Zoo That Grew, safe and sound, once and for all. Circle of life, indeed.

 We Can't Wait to See You! 
 
 As one of Alabama’s favorite family attractions, Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo is an exciting place to visit with a lot happening every day. We can’t wait for you to visit! 
 
 
 
 
 We're Open 9 am- 4 pm Daily 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 We are open every day of the week except on major US holidays- Christmas, New Year’s Day, and Thanksgiving Day! 
 
 
 
 
 Ticket Information 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 Come visit us at Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo! Parking is free and we welcome groups of all sizes! 
 
 
 
 
 
 Adults & Teens (13-61) | $23.95
 
 
 
 
 Seniors (62+) | $20.95
 
 
 
 
 Children (3-12) | $15.95
 
 
 
 
 Children under 2 | Free!
 
 
 
 
 
 
 buy tickets!
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Animals Adventures With Sloths or Lemurs Available Daily! 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 Each adventure is $24.95 per person, plus a regular paid zoo admission, weather permitting. 
 
 
 
 Learn About Adventures
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Giraffe Feedings Twice A Day! 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 $5 per person, plus a regular paid zoo admission, weather permitting. 
 
 
 
 
 Some Features Are Currently Closed 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 These features are currently unavailable:Our Coola Springs Walkabout (Kangaroo) encounter is currently closed. You can learn more about Kangaroos on our Animals page! 
 
 
 
 
 We Offer A Discount To Locals! 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 10% off regular admission for Baldwin County Locals with ID. 
 
 
 
 
 Educational Rate Information 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 We offer a discounted admission rate of $8.00 per person with a minimum of 15 students and chaperones. Teachers and bus drivers get in free and there’s no minimum for daycare groups. Advance reservations are required. Ask about adding an educational program to your visit. 
 
 
 
 The Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo is the coolest classroom ever!Zoology, biology, ecology, geology, geography, conservation… Where else can teachers bring students of all ages to one unique place, surrounded by over 600 exotic animals, to learn about the amazing variety of life or “bio-diversity” of Planet Earth? We welcome both public and private school groups.Something magical happens when human beings get up close and personal with creatures they might otherwise never get to meet beyond a computer or TV screen. Curiosity and imagination are given flight here every day and we think those are great educational building blocks.Our zookeepers provide easy-to-understand science-based information and fun factoids about our zoo animals that will energize kids to keep learning, both inside and outside of the classroom. We hope we can inspire teachers too. 
 
 Explore Our Extra-Special Educational Experiences 
 
 
 
 Animal Adventures
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Keeper Presentations
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Our Animals
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Group Rate Information 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 We’re happy to accommodate most types: civic, community, church, tourist, employee, service organizations, and membership clubs. Groups require a minimum of 15 people to receive 15% off regular admission. A reservation at least 48 hours before arrival is required. 
 
 
 
 Additional InformationAll school groups and other educational groups receive a special discounted rate of $8 per person, paid staff is free. We require a reservation at least 48 hours prior to arrival. Call 251-256-7008 any time between 9am & 4pm. Be sure to ask about how to get an Educational Program added to your trip for a small additional fee.*Publicly funded school (K5-12, community college or university) are exempt from Alabama State Sales and Use Tax. Teachers and bus drivers receive free admission, but chaperones are charged admission.** Civic, church or non-profit organizations that are exempt or may qualify for exemption from Alabama State Sales and Use Tax are required to provide documentation at the time of reservation. 
 
 
 
 
 Gift Shop & Online Orders 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 We have an awesome gift shop! Please call 251-256-7008 or email retail@algulfcoastzoo.org for more information!  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Wanting to have your event at Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo? 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 Visit our Venue Rental page! From weddings to birthdays, corporate gatherings, and any celebration in between, the Zoo is the perfect fit for your next event.

 About The Zoo 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Mission Statement 
 
 The mission of the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo is to create compelling experiences that connect people and community with wildlife, and inspire personal responsibility for conservation of the natural world. Education. Conservation. Adventure. Community. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 About The Zoo 
 
 The zoo is about 6 miles from the beach. Tucked just off the main highway, visitors feel like they have entered a tropical urban oasis filled with intriguing sounds from our rich diversity of exotic animals. Whether it’s the distinctive call from our peacocks or chatter from our monkeys you are instantly transported out of life’s hustle and bustle into our peaceful kingdom.Voted the “#1 Zoo in Alabama” for two years running!If you really want something extra unforgettable, stop in for a one-on-one, up-close experience with a few of our friendliest friends at our Animal Encounters!

 Safety First 
 
 The safety of every zoo visitor, our staff, and our animals have precedence over everything at the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo. We follow every safety protocol as required by law, and receive 100% compliance by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), the federal agency that annually inspects our facility. We maintain ongoing safety training procedures in the handling of our animals by our keepers, and stay vigilant in keeping our facility structures secure. We take great pride in our constant efforts to provide the safest and most secure environment we can for your family when you come to visit ours. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Sources of Revenue 
 
 As a non-profit 501(c)(3) organization, the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo relies solely on admissions, memberships, and contributions to remain in business.  
 
 Construction of the new Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo is an on going project and our Philanthropy Partnership Program plays an extremely significant role.It ensures that the zoo becomes a prominent member of an ever-growing business and civic community in its new Gulf Shores location, while offering education, entertainment, and cultural activities, especially for families.By participating in one of the zoo’s many partnership programs, you, your company, organization, or institution can contribute to the zoo’s vibrant, secure standing far into the future.

If you’ve been following the journey of our two new red wolves, Jenkins and Walker, we have a wonderful milestone to share. Jenkins has been spotted exploring the yard of his habitat during the day.

Want to learn more about these critically endangered wolves? Come visit the Zoo and see conservation in action.

 DYK?
Red wolves are one of the most critically endangered canids in the world.
A few key facts:
* Fewer than 20 red wolves remain in the wild today, all in eastern North Carolina.
* A little over 200 red wolves live under human care in zoos and wildlife centers.
* The SAFE (Saving Animals From Extinction) American Red Wolf Program works to research, breed, and prepare these wolves for potential release back into the wild.

Animal Ambassador Walkabout: 10:45 am – 11:15 am. Starts at the Event Stage.
Discover the wonders of wildlife with the “Animal Ambassador Walkabout” at the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo! Join our expert handlers as they stroll through the zoo with a variety of fascinating animal ambassadors. This unique experience offers an up-close encounter with some of our most captivating creatures, including reptiles, mammals, and birds. Learn about each ambassador’s natural habitat, behaviors, and the vital conservation efforts aimed at protecting their species. Engage with our knowledgeable staff, ask questions, and marvel at the incredible adaptations that help these animals thrive. The “Animal Ambassador Walkabout” is a must-see, offering an enriching, educational, and unforgettable adventure for visitors of all ages!

Gulf Shores hidden gem.

I really want half my money back.  Nothing was really open .  Almost all the animals was gone or inside .  No food bar , the best thing was feeding the animals.  This was a waste of time and really doesn’t deserve a rating.  If you are not going to be able to give what you advertise please stop .  Thank you

Animal Ambassador Walkabout: 10:45 am – 11:15 am. Starts at the Event Stage.
Discover the wonders of wildlife with the “Animal Ambassador Walkabout” at the Alabama Gulf Coast Zoo! Join our expert handlers as they stroll through the zoo with a variety of fascinating animal ambassadors. This unique experience offers an up-close encounter with some of our most captivating creatures, including reptiles, mammals, and birds. Learn about each ambassador’s natural habitat, behaviors, and the vital conservation efforts aimed at protecting their species. Engage with our knowledgeable staff, ask questions, and marvel at the incredible adaptations that help these animals thrive. The “Animal Ambassador Walkabout” is a must-see, offering an enriching, educational, and unforgettable adventure for visitors of all ages!

* Protecting red wolves helps protect entire ecosystems by keeping populations of deer, raccoons, and rodents in balance.Read more21/5Alabama Gulf Coast ZooMarch 14, 2026ViewWe’re out and about at the BB-Q & Blues Cook Off in Downtown Foley!

Come on out and see us — we’ve brought some of our favorite Animal Ambassadors along for the fun!

Say hello to Rose the opossum, Lucy the three‑banded armadillo, Mia the Central American boa, and Mailbox the box turtle. They’re soaking up the sunshine, the music, and all the friendly faces.

If you’re wandering the festival today, swing by and visit. We’d love to see you!

review.reviewBody: Nice
Gulf Shores hidden gem.

Really fun time with the family here. Clean inside the buildings and the staff was nice to us. We had a group of 12 😅  Do you guys have a link for purchasing merchandise online? My son retrospectively would like a T-shirt but we&#039;re back home now in TX lol

Kids fed the giraffe! Honestly the only disappointing thing was the cost of the stuffed animals. $25 a piece? I would&#039;ve gotten em but I&#039;m not spending $100 (4 kiddos) on a regular stuffed animal.

I really want half my money back.  Nothing was really open .  Almost all the animals was gone or inside .  No food bar , the best thing was feeding the animals.  This was a waste of time and really doesn’t deserve a rating.  If you are not going to be able to give what you advertise please stop .  Thank you
A bit on the small side for the cost of admission. Imo BUT has lots of small monkeys monkeys and all the cats Displays are well laid out as we could see all the critters
The animals were well cared for. It was a very pretty zoo with lots of very neat animals.

What staff we came across were friendly, most animals were lazy, &amp; didn&#039;t move around, it was a warm day, but still?? Anything extra like walking in the lemuer enclosure was x-tra ( $25 )  prices were way high, not worth the price. So underwhelmed with my experience.
Okay,  very nice,  clean and friendly.  Nice paths to stroll. Could have more benches and more animals. Sad to say but needs more animals.

Perfect size zoo, you can see every exhibit in a morning or afternoon. Great variety of monkeys and cats. But they have a surprising amount of other animals. You can buy tickets to feed the giraffes too.
The worst zoo we went there 6 moths ago and the cashier was just horribly disrespectful. The zoo is too expensive the enclosures were dirty.
